source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory 6(2) - Exp 1
finding: Theory: overconfidence comes partly from justifying the chosen answer and ignoring contradicting evidence. Test: two-alternative general-knowledge questions. In the reasons condition people first listed and rated reasons for and against both options, then chose and gave a probability. Calibration improved clearly. Some overconfidence stayed, mostly at .9 and 1.0.
numbers: 73 paid volunteers; 6 sets of 10 questions; control vs reasons condition; Brier score and Murphy partition used; groups compared by jackknife. Table values not recoverable from the text extract.
limits: Short question sets; general-knowledge almanac items only. Order of control and reasons blocks was checked and did not explain the gain.
agent_relevance: Forcing a written case against the chosen answer before stating confidence is a calibration tool for a model too. It fits a check that fires on a signal, not on a schedule (G1).

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory 6(2) - Exp 2
finding: Simplified manipulation: choose first, then write one reason. Only listing a contradicting reason improved calibration. Listing a supporting reason did nothing, so supporting reasons are what people already do. Writing one of each helped slightly and not significantly.
numbers: 200 paid volunteers; same 6 sets of 10 questions; 4 groups (supporting, contradicting, both, control). 11 subjects dropped from the contradicting group for writing supporting reasons; result held when they were kept. Effect: proportion correct up a little, mean probability down a little.
limits: Contradicting gain was smaller than the full reasons task of Exp 1. People found a contradicting reason hard to write.
agent_relevance: Asking a model to argue for its answer adds nothing. Asking for the strongest reason against does. Only the contradicting prompt has measured value, and it works best when tied to real evidence.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory 6(2) - both/reversed control
finding: Why did the both group not improve when Exp 1 did? Test of order: 44 new subjects gave one reason for each alternative BEFORE choosing. Still no improvement over control. Order was not the cause. Contradicting reasons in the both group were often weak, so the two effects were not additive.
numbers: 44 subjects; 35 control items then 30 items in the modified both condition. Authors say they could not stop covert early choice.
limits: Null result; small sample; shows the effect is fragile to how reasons are produced.
agent_relevance: Balanced pro and con prompts can wash out the gain. Test any critic step against a plain control, and prefer one focused counter-argument.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory 6(2) - analysis of reasons
finding: People search memory for supporting reasons more than against. Reasons for were more plentiful and rated stronger than reasons against.
numbers: 62 subjects after 6 dropped; 3.17 reasons per question; 18.3 reasons for vs 13.4 against per subject (t(61)=7.99, p<.001); at least one reason for on 14.7 of 20 alternatives vs 12.3 against (t(61)=6.04); first reason for rated 3.8 vs against 3.5 (t(61)=2.92, p<.005).
limits: Self-reported reasons from almanac questions; 7-point strength ratings are subjective.
agent_relevance: Positive-evidence bias is built into how a chooser gathers evidence. A model drafting its own justification will show the same skew; counter-evidence must be requested explicitly.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory 6(2) - what drives confidence
finding: Confidence tracks the amount and strength of evidence supporting the chosen answer, not evidence against it. Two-stage view: search knowledge until an answer is chosen, then review evidence and assess confidence. One bias in each stage.
numbers: Pooled n=620 answers. Correlation of confidence with number of reasons: .28 for-chosen, .17 against-rejected, -.06 for-rejected, -.07 against-chosen. With strength of first reason: .66, .39, .00, -.02. Mean probability below .6 when for-chosen strength under 3, about .9 at strength 7. Choice of option correlated .61 with the count difference of for-reasons.
limits: Correlational, not causal. Items were two-choice trivia.
agent_relevance: Confidence read off the support for the answer, ignoring disconfirming evidence, predicts overconfidence. Score should count the strongest counter-reason, not a self-reported number.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory 6(2) - literature recap
finding: The paper restates the founding facts (Lichtenstein, Fischhoff and Phillips 1977; Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein 1977) and an early training study. Feedback training can help but did not generalise to new content, so the problem is not only mapping feelings to numbers.
numbers: Typical: hit rate .6 at assessed .70; at .90 about 75% correct; p=1.00 answers wrong about 20% of the time; people risked money on them. Training: 11 sessions of 200 items with feedback; almost all gain came after the first feedback round.
limits: Second-hand recap inside a 1980 paper; the training study (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff, in press) was not opened.
agent_relevance: Calibration learned on one content type may not carry to another. Calibrate per task type from outcomes, not once globally.

source: Plous (1993) The Psychology of Judgment and Decision Making, ch. 19 Overconfidence (web copy) - Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein 1977
finding: Founding result as summarised by Plous: extreme certainty is often wrong. Three follow-ups (after a lecture, hypothetical bets, real bets) all showed the gap. Real money did not remove it.
numbers: Certainty answers 70-85% correct. Odds near 3:1 aligned with accuracy. 100:1 odds gave 73% correct. 10,000:1 to 1,000,000:1 gave 85-90% correct (should be about 6:1 to 9:1). Replication 2: 39 of 42 accepted bets. Replication 3: 13 of 19 gambled, 12% wrong on items rated 50:1 or better; losses $1-$11 each.
limits: Secondary source; figures relayed, original not read here; original sample sizes not given.
agent_relevance: Extreme stated certainty is the least reliable region. Ignore stated certainty above a threshold unless backed by held-out checks (G3).

source: Plous (1993) ch. 19 - Lichtenstein and Fischhoff 1977; Lichtenstein, Fischhoff, Phillips 1982; Oskamp 1965
finding: Overconfidence is largest near chance and shrinks as accuracy rises; above about 80% accuracy people turn underconfident (hard-easy effect). For interval tasks the surprise rate far exceeds the 2% implied by 98% intervals.
numbers: Lichtenstein and Fischhoff 1977: 65-70% confidence when about 50% right; children's drawings 53% right vs 68% confident; stocks 47% right vs 65% confident. Surprise index averaged 32% over nearly 15,000 judgments (98% intervals). Russo and Schoemaker: over 1,000 people, under 1% got 9 or 10 of 10 intervals; surprise index 40-70%. Oskamp 1965: 32 subjects, accuracy 26% vs confidence 33%, over 90% overconfident after part 4.
limits: Secondary source. The hard-easy effect is partly a regression artifact (Erev et al. 1994, not opened).
agent_relevance: Overconfidence depends on difficulty. Expect worst miscalibration on hard items; more information raised confidence not accuracy (Oskamp).

source: Plous (1993) ch. 19 - experts and training
finding: Calibration is domain-specific. Weather forecasters (daily feedback) are almost perfectly calibrated; physicians diagnosing pneumonia were poorly calibrated. Feedback can cure overconfidence.
numbers: Murphy and Winkler 1984: forecasters near perfect. Christensen-Szalanski and Bushyhead 1981: large overconfidence. Lichtenstein and Fischhoff 1980: better after 200 judgments with intensive feedback. Arkes et al. 1987: overconfidence removed after feedback on five deceptively hard problems.
limits: Secondary source; no numbers given for bridge players or oddsmakers.
agent_relevance: Fast outcome feedback on the same task type makes calibration good. An agent with test results to check against can recalibrate; one without cannot.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein (1977) Knowing with certainty: the appropriateness of extreme confidence. JEP:HPP 3(4)
finding: Original founding paper. Fetch was blocked (403). Search snippets, Koriat 1980 and Plous say: answers given with certainty (p=1.00) were wrong about 20% of the time, and odds of 10,000:1 to 1,000,000:1 were right only 85-90% of the time.
numbers: Only secondary figures; see the Plous and Koriat lines for numbers I did read.
limits: NOT opened. Do not cite original N or conditions from this line.
agent_relevance: Same as the Plous line on Fischhoff 1977.

source: Wikipedia: Overconfidence effect (secondary summary)
finding: Secondary list of classic numbers: spelling task, general knowledge, 90% interval tasks.
numbers: Adams and Adams 1960 spelling: about 80% correct at claimed 100% certainty. Lichtenstein, Fischhoff, Phillips 1982: wrong 20% when 100% certain. Alpert and Raiffa 1982: 90% intervals hit as low as 50%. Svenson 1981: 93% of US drivers above median. Oskamp 1965: confidence 33% to 53% with more info, accuracy under 30%.
limits: Encyclopedia page; primary papers not checked. Gigerenzer, Kruger, hard-easy items had no numbers on the page.
agent_relevance: Interval hit rate near 50% for nominal 90% is a clean benchmark for LLM interval tests.

source: Gigerenzer, Hoffrage, Kleinbolting (1991) Probabilistic mental models: a Brunswikian theory of confidence. Psych Review 98(4)
finding: Competing theory (from abstract-level snippets). People answer a two-choice question from memory using a probabilistic mental model: a reference class and cues with ecological validity. Confidence is the validity of the cue used. Overconfidence appears when items are not randomly sampled from the reference class and should vanish with representative sampling. Predicts a confidence-frequency effect: judged frequency of own correct answers is more accurate than single-item confidence.
numbers: Abstract-level only. Exp 1 figures NOT read (PDF blocked: 403/Cloudflare). No numbers recorded.
limits: NOT opened. Critics say PMM assumptions are questionable (search snippet).
agent_relevance: Calibration depends on how test items are sampled. Judge an agent's confidence on a representative task mix, not hand-picked hard items.

source: Juslin (1994) The overconfidence phenomenon as a consequence of informal experimenter-guided selection of almanac items. OBHDP 57
finding: Known as the main support for the item-selection explanation: randomly sampled almanac items show little overconfidence, hand-picked items show much. Only the OpenAlex record (about 325 citations) was seen; the result is from title and background knowledge.
numbers: NOT read. No magnitudes recorded.
limits: NOT opened. Brenner et al. 1996 (Overconfidence in probability and frequency judgments, about 300 citations) later argued overconfidence persists beyond selection; also not opened (ScienceDirect blocked).
agent_relevance: Dispute over item selection is a boundary condition: measure the agent on its real item distribution.

source: Moore and Healy (2008) The trouble with overconfidence. Psych Review 115
finding: Splits overconfidence into overestimation, overplacement and overprecision. Bayesian account with noisy private information predicts overestimation on hard tasks and underestimation on easy ones, and the reverse for overplacement. (From record and background knowledge; paper not read.)
numbers: NOT read (SSRN fetch blocked). About 2,500 citations in OpenAlex.
limits: NOT opened. No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Score three things separately for an agent: accuracy overstated, rank overstated, intervals too narrow.

source: Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger (2017) On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML
finding: Modern deep nets are overconfident even though more accurate. A 5-layer LeNet is calibrated; a 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-100 is not (confidence well above accuracy). Defines ECE with M=15 bins and reliability diagrams. One scalar temperature T fitted on a validation set by NLL fixes most of it and does not change accuracy.
numbers: ECE before vs after temperature scaling: Birds ResNet50 9.19% to 1.85%; Cars ResNet50 4.3% to 2.35%; CIFAR-10 ResNet110 4.6% to 0.83%; CIFAR-10 LeNet5 3.02% to 0.93%. Histogram binning and BBQ about as good on some sets.
limits: Classification with softmax; vision and some NLP sets. Not about generated text. Matrix scaling overfits (21.13% on Birds).
agent_relevance: A cheap post-hoc rescaling of confidence, fitted on held-out outcomes, beats fancy prompting. This is code selecting (G5), not model opinion.

source: Guo et al. (2017) - causes of miscalibration
finding: Capacity and training choices raise miscalibration: more depth, more width, Batch Normalization, and less weight decay. NLL overfits while error keeps falling, so confidence grows without accuracy.
numbers: CIFAR-100 ResNets (depth varied up to 110 layers; width varied at fixed depth 14). Exact slopes are in figures, not in text.
limits: Mechanism evidence is correlational across architectures.
agent_relevance: Bigger or longer-trained models do not buy honest confidence; measure calibration again whenever the model changes.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know. Anthropic
finding: Large pretrained LMs are well calibrated on multiple choice and True/False questions in the right format; calibration improves with size and with few-shot over zero-shot. Replacing an option with none of the above hurts accuracy and calibration. RLHF policies look miscalibrated but become fairly calibrated with a temperature change.
numbers: 10-bin ECE; models up to 52B; RLHF policy shown at T=1 vs T=2.5 on MMLU, MMLU True/False, TruthfulQA (5-shot, 52B).
limits: Calibration depends on prompt format. RLHF miscalibration is partly a temperature issue, which Tian et al. later question.
agent_relevance: Answer format matters for confidence. Prefer fixed multiple-choice or True/False probes and normalise over options in code (G5).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) - P(True) self-evaluation and P(IK)
finding: Models can grade their own samples with P(True), which is harder because models find their own samples plausible. Few-shot k mostly improves calibration, not AUROC. Showing many of the model's own T=1 samples before judging one improves self-evaluation (like self-consistency). A trained P(IK) head predicts which questions the model can answer but transfers only partly and is poorly calibrated out of distribution.
numbers: Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, HumanEval, arithmetic, function synthesis. P(IK) trained on TriviaQA; AUROC rises with model size. P(IK) rises with source material and correct hints, falls with distracting hints.
limits: Only partial generalisation; Anthropic models up to 52B.
agent_relevance: Agreement among own samples is a useful hint (G4: a hint, never proof). A learned do-I-know signal helps routing but needs recalibration per task.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words. TMLR
finding: A GPT-3 model fine-tuned to write a confidence level after its answer is calibrated, and stays moderately calibrated under distribution shift. It uses its own uncertainty, not copied human examples. Verbalized and logit-based confidence both generalise.
numbers: CalibratedMath: trained on Add-subtract, tested on Multi-answer and Multiply-divide. Median accuracy 21% on Add-subtract vs 65% on Multi-answer (label shift). Table 1 rows include indirect logit MSE/MAD 22.0/16.4 (Multi-answer) and 10.4/9.4 (Multiply-divide); constant baseline 33.7/38.4 and 15.3/8.5 (column alignment of the text extract is uncertain).
limits: Fine-tuned GPT-3 on arithmetic only; zero-shot answers held fixed.
agent_relevance: First evidence that stated confidence can be trained to track real uncertainty. Training is outside our scope; scoring confidence against outcomes is in scope.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration. EMNLP - gpt-3.5-turbo
finding: For RLHF chat models, asking for a number or word-level likelihood in the output beats the model's token probabilities. Relative ECE cut often about 50%.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo ECE on TriviaQA / SciQ / TruthfulQA: label prob .140 / .256 / .451; Is-True prob .164 / .312 / .470; verbalized one-stage top-4 .054 / .065 / .203; top-1 .068 / .234 / .389; two-stage CoT .110 / .323 / .419. AUC on TriviaQA: label prob .869 vs verbalized top-4 .896.
limits: Three benchmarks, closed models, mid-2023. AUC gains are small; most of the ECE gain is calibration, not discrimination. TruthfulQA stays poor.
agent_relevance: Disagrees with Kadavath on RLHF: for chat models verbalized confidence can beat logits. Both stay only an input to code-based selection.

source: Tian et al. (2023) - top-k and Claude-1
finding: Asking for several candidate answers each with a probability (top-k) improves calibration; authors tie this to considering the opposite. Claude-1 log-probs were as good as gpt-3.5, but it verbalized worse, so verbalized calibration depends on the model family.
numbers: Claude-1 ECE TriviaQA / SciQ / TruthfulQA: label prob .074 / .216 / .432; verbalized 1S top-1 .049 / .265 / .440; top-2 .046 / .207 / .450; top-4 .075 / .151 / .372. gpt-3.5 SciQ ECE falls .234 (top-1) to .065 (top-4).
limits: Claude-1 is deprecated; top-k effect not uniform across datasets.
agent_relevance: Mirrors Koriat 1980: listing alternatives (the counter-case) improves calibration. A forced distribution over exclusive answers summing to 1 supports G5.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? ICLR
finding: Vanilla verbalized confidence is overconfident and mimics human talk: values sit in 80-100% and in multiples of 5. Bigger models do better but are far from ideal. GPT-4 has lower ECE but is poor at telling right from wrong.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna 13B, LLaMA 2 70B) x 8 tasks. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC only 62.7% vs 50% chance. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
limits: Black-box prompting only; worst on professional-knowledge tasks (law).
agent_relevance: Verbalized certainty is mostly rhetoric. Confidence from agreement across samples is better than stated numbers.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) - strategies and white-box gap
finding: Human-inspired prompts, sampling several answers and aggregation (Avg-Conf, Pair-Rank) reduce overconfidence. No single method wins. White-box methods are better but the gap is narrow.
numbers: Pair-Rank reaches ECE as low as 0.028; Avg-Conf best at failure prediction. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 on average. Recommended: Top-K prompt + self-random sampling + Avg-Conf or Pair-Rank.
limits: Methods struggle on tasks needing professional knowledge; samples from one model are correlated.
agent_relevance: Supports using consistency across independent attempts as the confidence signal (a G4 hint) and doing the aggregation in code.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Dont Know. NeurIPS
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration for open-ended answers. Fine-tuning on a small graded set (LoRA) gives uncertainty that transfers across tasks and even across models. A user study shows calibrated uncertainty changes human reliance.
numbers: About a thousand graded examples suffice to beat baselines; LLaMA-2 7B/13B, Mistral 7B and chat variants; open-ended MMLU variant. Only the first pages of the PDF text extracted, so tables were not read.
limits: Needs weights and training; outside a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence from prompts is weak and outcome-graded data is the fix. Keep a log of graded outcomes and rescale confidence in code.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know. Nature Machine Intelligence
finding: Calibration gap: people overestimate LLM accuracy when given default explanations. Discrimination gap: people barely tell right from wrong answers from the explanation alone.
numbers: Model confidence AUC .751 (GPT-3.5) and .746 (PaLM2) on multiple choice, .781 (GPT-4o mini) on short answer; human confidence AUC only .589, .602, .592. 350 MMLU questions, model accuracy 55% (GPT-3.5) and 50% (PaLM2).
limits: Participant counts not recorded here; model confidence from token log-probs.
agent_relevance: Readers take fluency and length as certainty. Output should state measured confidence plainly; explanation length is not evidence.

source: Steyvers et al. - explanation style experiment
finding: Longer explanations raised human confidence even when accuracy did not rise. Matching explanation certainty wording to the model's real confidence narrowed both gaps.
numbers: With model-confidence-matched explanations the discrimination gap narrowed (BF > 100, 6.48, > 100 in Exp 2a, 2b, 2c). Where participants changed the LLM answer, they scored 33% vs LLM 39%; in other cases human accuracy was 51% vs LLM 52%.
limits: LLM calibration itself imperfect; multiple-choice LLM overconfident, short-answer LLM slightly underconfident.
agent_relevance: Aligning wording to measured confidence helps users. Do not let length or hedging style carry unmeasured signals.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky, Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the Grey Area: Expressions of Overconfidence and Uncertainty in Language Models
finding: LMs are very sensitive to certainty words injected in prompts. High-certainty phrases lower accuracy; hedges raise it. Likely mimicry of web text: uncertainty words go with answers, certainty words with questions.
numbers: 50 markers; accuracy varied by more than 80% across templates on the same questions; high-certainty expressions gave a 7% accuracy drop vs low certainty; TriviaQA 42% plain vs 56% with a double-check hedge; one template at 14% where others reached near-perfect.
limits: Older GPT-3/GPT-4-era models; effect on accuracy, not directly on calibration error.
agent_relevance: Confidence wording in the prompt or in the model's text shifts correctness. Avoid forcing be-sure language; confidence words are style, not state.

source: Cross-reading of Kadavath, Tian, Xiong, Lin, Kapoor (synthesis)
finding: Base models calibrate via logits; RLHF chat models calibrate better via verbalized numbers than logits (Tian) yet verbalized numbers cluster at 80-100% (Xiong); fine-tuning on graded outcomes is the most reliable fix (Lin, Kapoor).
numbers: Contrast: gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE .140 (label prob) vs .054 (verbalized top-4); Xiong average ECE above .377 for vanilla verbalized across 8 tasks. Both can hold because tasks and prompts differ.
limits: Different datasets, prompts and ECE binning; not directly comparable. No study here used an agent loop.
agent_relevance: Treat stated confidence as one weak feature; build the real signal from sample agreement, held-out checks and logged outcomes.
